transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I guess the main thing is my sleep. It’s gotten really, really messed up lately. Like, some nights I’m just up half the night, and it’s not even that I’m doing anything important—I’m just lying there with my mind running and running, like I can’t shut it off. And then other times I’ll wake up way too early, before I need to, and I feel like I barely slept at all. I’ll be exhausted, but not rested, if that makes sense.

It’s just started to feel like it’s affecting everything, and I don’t really know how to get it back under control.
When you’re lying awake, do you feel worried or anxious?

I’m not totally sure I’d call it worried, exactly. I mean, sometimes I’m thinking about things, like stuff I need to do or conversations from the day or whatever, but it doesn’t always feel like fear or panic. It’s more like my brain just won’t settle down, if that makes sense.

I don’t know if that counts as anxious. I’m not lying there thinking, “Oh no, something terrible is going to happen,” at least not usually. It’s more just... I’m awake, and my thoughts keep going, and then I start noticing that I’m still awake, and that gets frustrating. But I don’t know if I’d label it as anxiety.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

Yeah… I think so. I’ve been feeling pretty down lately, more than I want to admit, probably. It’s like I’ll wake up and before anything has even happened, there’s already this heavy, empty feeling sitting there. Not even like I’m reacting to a bad day—it’s just there.

And it’s weird because I’ll be in my own condo, which I worked so hard to get, and I know I should feel proud or comfortable or at least okay there. But lately I’ll just sit there and look around and it makes me want to cry. Not because anything specific is wrong with the place, just because I feel so… empty, I guess. Heavy and empty at the same time, if that makes sense.
Have you been getting less enjoyment from things you usually like to do?

Yeah… yeah, I have. That’s actually been one of the harder things to explain, because it’s not like I made some big decision to stop doing things. It’s more like I just… stopped.

I used to go to salsa class, and I really liked it. It was something I looked forward to, even if I was tired after work or didn’t feel like leaving the condo at first. Once I got there, the music and moving around and just being around people usually helped. But I haven’t been going. I keep telling myself, “Maybe next week,” or I’ll think about getting dressed for it, and then it feels like this huge amount of effort for something I don’t even feel excited about anymore.

And painting too. I have my paints still sitting out on the table, like I was going to use them. They’re just there. I’ll look at them and it feels strange, like they belong to somebody else. Like I remember that I’m the kind of person who likes painting, but I don’t actually feel it right now. I don’t get that little pull to sit down and start. I just look at everything and feel nothing, which is kind of scary because those were things that used to feel like me.
Have you had any thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of harming yourself?

I… I don’t really know how to answer that cleanly.

I don’t think I’m sitting there making plans to hurt myself or anything like that. It’s more that when I’m really low, I get this kind of thought like, “What is the point of all this?” or I feel tired of having to keep doing everything, if that makes sense. But then I second-guess whether that counts as life not feeling worth living, because it’s not like I’m picturing a specific thing or wanting to do something to myself.

It’s more… I just feel really worn down sometimes, and I don’t like admitting that out loud because it sounds dramatic. But I haven’t been, like, planning to harm myself.
Did this start after something stressful happened in your life?

I think… yeah, it kind of did. Not like one dramatic thing happened in a single day and then I woke up like this, but it seemed to get really obvious after the mortgage became real.

Buying the condo was supposed to be a good thing, and I know it is, but once the papers were signed and it wasn’t just an idea anymore, it felt like this huge weight landed on me. Like, okay, now this is mine, this payment is mine, this responsibility is mine. And since then—probably about a month now—I’ve noticed this really obvious back-and-forth, where I had that more charged-up stretch and then this crash after it. The crash part especially has been hard to ignore.

So I guess the stressful thing was the mortgage becoming real. It’s been about a month of this being noticeable.
During that more charged-up stretch, did you feel unusually energized or “up” compared with your normal self?

Yeah… I did. It’s hard to describe without making it sound like I was just in a good mood, because it wasn’t exactly that. It was more like I felt almost lit up, like everything in me was turned up higher than usual. I remember thinking, “Okay, I’ve got this, I can handle everything,” like I was suddenly unstoppable or something.

And at first that felt kind of good, honestly, especially compared to now. Like I had more confidence than I normally do, and things felt more possible. But it wasn’t just happy or positive. I was also really quick to get irritated. My mom would ask me a normal question, something small, and I’d snap back like she was accusing me of something. Or my supervisor would ask about some little detail at work, and I’d feel this flash of anger, like, “Why are you on me about this?” even though normally I probably would’ve just answered.

So yes, I was more “up,” but also kind of edgy with it. Not calm energy. More like I was running hot.
During that more charged-up stretch, did you need less sleep than usual and still feel okay the next day?

Yeah. That was one of the weirdest parts, honestly, because normally if I don’t sleep enough, I feel it right away. I’m dragging, I need coffee, I’m kind of useless in the morning.

But during that stretch, there were several nights where I only slept maybe three or four hours, and I still got up feeling… charged, I guess. Like I’d wake up and my body was already going, like I didn’t even need coffee. I remember almost being surprised by it, because I’d look at the time and realize how little I’d slept, but I didn’t feel tired in the way I should have.

It wasn’t like I was resting well, exactly. It was more like sleep just didn’t feel as necessary for a bit, which is not normal for me.
During that more charged-up stretch, were you doing more activities or taking on more projects than usual?

Yeah, definitely. That was actually one of the things that made me realize something was off, because it wasn’t just that I had more energy in my head — I was doing a lot more.

I’d get home from work, and normally after staring at numbers all day I want to eat something, maybe watch TV, maybe do one chore if I’m being responsible. But during that stretch, I’d come home and suddenly start cleaning like the place had to be fixed immediately. I’d be wiping down cabinets, sorting things, moving stuff around, like I couldn’t just sit down.

And then because of the condo, I started making all these renovation lists — not even realistic ones, necessarily. Like I’d be writing down what I wanted to change, what it might cost, what order to do things in, looking up supplies, comparing ideas. Then I’d switch over to checking interest rates again, even though the mortgage was already done, like I needed to keep monitoring everything.

And on top of that I started setting up ideas for side jobs, like ways I could bring in extra money. I’d be making notes, looking at options, thinking maybe I could do bookkeeping on the side or organize something online. It was all after work, too. It wasn’t like I had free time. I just kept going like I couldn’t shut it off.
About how many days in a row did that more charged-up period last?

I’m trying to count it exactly, because it wasn’t like one clean block where I can say, “It started Monday and ended Friday.” The really obvious back-and-forth — like being all charged up and then crashing — has been going on for about a month now, basically since the mortgage became real and it wasn’t just an idea anymore.

The charged-up parts would come in stretches within that, but the whole pattern has been about a month. That’s when I started noticing, or maybe when it became harder to ignore, because everything felt more intense around then.
During those charged-up periods, were you talking more than usual?

Yeah… I think so. I didn’t notice it at first as “talking more,” exactly, because in my head it felt like I was just explaining things that were important. But my sister definitely noticed.

I remember one conversation where I was going on about the condo stuff, and it was like I jumped from equity to taxes to paint colors and then back to what I should do first, and she finally kind of laughed but also looked overwhelmed and said I was talking really fast. Like she couldn’t even get a word in.

And I could feel it, too, once she pointed it out. It was like there was this pressure behind it, like if I didn’t keep going I’d lose the thread or the idea would disappear. I wasn’t trying to cut her off, but I kept pushing forward, almost like the words were coming faster than I could sort them.
During those charged-up periods, did you feel more confident or capable than usual—to the point that your ideas or abilities seemed unusually strong or special?

Yeah… yes, I think that’s a good way to put it. At the time it didn’t feel like “I’m being unrealistic” or anything. It felt like I could just handle everything if I pushed hard enough.

I honestly started thinking I could pay the condo down really fast, like way faster than a normal person probably would with my income, and that I’d just figure it out somehow. And then I’d be thinking, okay, I can study for the CPA exams too, even though that’s a huge thing and I haven’t exactly had some perfect plan for it before. But during those charged-up times it was like, no, I can do that, I can pass them, I can move up, I can make more money.

And then I also got really convinced I could run a little bookkeeping business on the side, like after work, and somehow it would all fit together. Condo, extra payments, CPA studying, side clients — in my head it wasn’t even “maybe.” It was more like, of course I can do this, failure just isn’t an option.

Looking back, it feels kind of embarrassing because I know those are big things, and not impossible exactly, but the way I was thinking about them was… too certain. Like I suddenly had this belief that I was much more capable than usual and that if I just kept going, I’d make it all happen.
During those charged-up periods, did you do anything unusually risky or impulsive for you?

I’m not really sure how to answer that, honestly. I don’t think there was anything like… clearly dangerous, if that’s what you mean. Like I didn’t do something that immediately makes me think, “Oh, that was reckless.”

But I also keep second-guessing myself, because some things felt impulsive in the moment just because I was moving so fast mentally. Like I’d get an idea and feel this urge to act on it right away, instead of sitting with it or thinking it through the way I normally would. So I guess it depends on what counts as risky.

I don’t have one big example where I can say, “Yes, that was definitely risky.” It was more that I felt less cautious than usual, but I’m not sure I actually did anything that crossed a line.
Did any one of those charged-up periods last for 4 days in a row or longer?

Yeah… I think so. It’s a little hard for me to pin down cleanly, because it hasn’t felt like one neat episode with a start and stop, if that makes sense. But the really obvious back-and-forth — like being in that charged-up stretch and then kind of crashing afterward — has been going on for about a month now.

It really started once the mortgage became real. Like, once it wasn’t just an abstract condo thing anymore, my brain sort of latched onto it, and since then I’ve noticed the cycling a lot more. So I can’t give you an exact day-by-day answer off the top of my head, but yes, there were definitely stretches in there that felt like they lasted several days, not just one afternoon or one night.
During one of those charged-up periods, did it cause problems at work or in your relationships?

Yeah… it has, I think. Not in a dramatic way where I stopped functioning completely, because I’m still showing up to work and doing my job, mostly. But it’s definitely started to show.

At work, I’ve made reconciliation mistakes that I really shouldn’t be making. Like, that’s literally part of what I do, so it’s not the kind of thing I can just brush off as, “Oh, everyone makes mistakes.” I mean, everyone does, obviously, but these were enough that my supervisor pulled me aside and asked what was going on. She wasn’t cruel about it, but it was embarrassing. I felt like I had to act like I was fine, but inside I was kind of panicking because I knew I wasn’t being as careful as I normally am.

And socially… yeah, I’ve been avoiding people more. I usually go to salsa class, and I’ve skipped it, and I’ve been dodging friends or not really answering messages the way I normally would. It’s not that they did anything wrong. I just don’t feel like myself, and I don’t want to have to explain that, or be around people and feel like they can tell something is off with me. So I guess it has caused problems, even if I’ve been trying to keep everything looking normal from the outside.
During those charged-up periods, did other people notice that you were unusually active or driven compared with your normal self?

Yeah… I think so. I don’t know if anyone said it in those exact words, like, “You’re unusually driven,” but I think it was noticeable because I was doing way more than I normally would after work.

Like for a while I’d come home and instead of just making dinner or watching something and going to bed, I’d suddenly have this burst of energy and I’d start cleaning, then making these detailed renovation lists for the condo, then checking interest rates again, then thinking through side-job ideas and setting things up like I had to do it right then. It wasn’t just one productive evening. It was more like I couldn’t shut it off once I got going.

And I think people could tell because I’d talk about all these plans and jump from one thing to another, and it probably sounded like a lot. I remember feeling almost irritated if someone slowed me down or acted like maybe I should just relax, because to me it felt urgent and important. So… yeah, compared with my normal self, I was definitely more active and kind of driven.
During those charged-up periods, did you spend money in ways that were unusual for you?

I’m not really sure. I mean… I don’t think there was anything huge, like I didn’t go buy a car or max out a credit card or anything like that. But I also feel like my sense of what was “reasonable” got kind of fuzzy during those periods, if that makes sense.

I remember looking at things for the condo and feeling like, “Well, we’re going to need this anyway,” or “This is an investment,” and I’d spend a lot of time comparing prices and putting things in carts. I don’t know that I actually bought a ton of it, though. That’s the part I’d have to check, because some of it was more browsing and planning than actually spending.

So… unusual? Maybe a little, but I don’t have a clear example where I’m like, yes, that was completely out of character and caused a big problem. I’d say I haven’t noticed anything major with spending, at least not the way the other stuff has stood out.
During any of those charged-up periods, were you hospitalized for your mood or behavior?

No… I’ve never been hospitalized for it. I mean, there have been times where I felt like I wasn’t handling things well, and I’ve gotten scared by how unlike myself I felt, but it never got to the point where I was taken to a hospital or admitted or anything like that.

I’ve always still been kind of… keeping it together on the outside, I guess. Maybe not well, but enough that it didn’t become an emergency in that way. So no, no hospitalizations for my mood or behavior.
During this low period, has your appetite changed a lot?

Yeah… it has, actually. I wouldn’t say I’m, like, carefully tracking my meals or my weight, but I’ve noticed I’m just not eating normally.

Dinner is the main thing. I’ll get home and I’ll mean to make something, or I’ll think, “Okay, I should eat,” but then I just don’t really have the appetite for it. Or it feels like too much effort, and I end up just eating crackers or something small while I’m sitting there with my budget notebook open. Like, not even a real meal, just picking at something because I know I should have food in my stomach.

And I can tell it’s not just in my head because my work pants feel looser than they did a few weeks ago. Not dramatically, maybe, but enough that I noticed it when I was getting dressed. So yeah… my appetite has been off, and I think I’ve probably lost some weight, even if I haven’t really weighed myself.
For at least 2 weeks in a row, have you felt depressed or lost interest in things most of the day, nearly every day?

Yeah… yes. I think so. It’s been more than two weeks, I’d say, where most days I wake up and there’s just this heavy, empty feeling already there, before anything has even happened.

It’s hard to explain because it’s not always like I’m actively crying all day, but it’s like everything feels flattened and sad underneath. Even being in my condo, which I worked so hard for and used to feel proud of, I’ll just sit there and look around and feel this awful emptiness, like it should make me happy and instead it makes me want to cry.

And it’s not just a bad evening here and there. It’s been pretty constant lately, most of the day. I keep thinking maybe if I get through work or get home or organize something I’ll feel different, but the feeling is still there. So… yeah, I’d say depressed is the word for it.

doctor.question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that my sleep has gotten really messed up—I’ll either stay up half the night with my mind running or wake up way too early feeling like I never rested.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I’m returning the chief complaint symptom code.

patient.answer:
I guess the main thing is my sleep. It’s gotten really, really messed up lately. Like, some nights I’m just up half the night, and it’s not even that I’m doing anything important—I’m just lying there with my mind running and running, like I can’t shut it off. And then other times I’ll wake up way too early, before I need to, and I feel like I barely slept at all. I’ll be exhausted, but not rested, if that makes sense.

It’s just started to feel like it’s affecting everything, and I don’t really know how to get it back under control.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure I’d call it worried, exactly. I mean, sometimes I’m thinking about things, like stuff I need to do or conversations from the day or whatever, but it doesn’t always feel like fear or panic. It’s more like my brain just won’t settle down, if that makes sense.

I don’t know if that counts as anxious. I’m not lying there thinking, “Oh no, something terrible is going to happen,” at least not usually. It’s more just... I’m awake, and my thoughts keep going, and then I start noticing that I’m still awake, and that gets frustrating. But I don’t know if I’d label it as anxiety.

doctor.intent: Assess loss of interest or pleasure to distinguish a depressive episode from primary insomnia, anxiety, or a stress-related condition.
doctor.question: Have you been getting less enjoyment from things you usually like to do?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I stopped going to salsa class and my paints are still sitting out on the table, but I look at them and feel nothing, like they belong to somebody else.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about reduced enjoyment or pleasure in usual activities, which directly matches loss of interest.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yeah, I have. That’s actually been one of the harder things to explain, because it’s not like I made some big decision to stop doing things. It’s more like I just… stopped.

I used to go to salsa class, and I really liked it. It was something I looked forward to, even if I was tired after work or didn’t feel like leaving the condo at first. Once I got there, the music and moving around and just being around people usually helped. But I haven’t been going. I keep telling myself, “Maybe next week,” or I’ll think about getting dressed for it, and then it feels like this huge amount of effort for something I don’t even feel excited about anymore.

And painting too. I have my paints still sitting out on the table, like I was going to use them. They’re just there. I’ll look at them and it feels strange, like they belong to somebody else. Like I remember that I’m the kind of person who likes painting, but I don’t actually feel it right now. I don’t get that little pull to sit down and start. I just look at everything and feel nothing, which is kind of scary because those were things that used to feel like me.

doctor.question: During that more charged-up stretch, did you feel unusually energized or “up” compared with your normal self?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Earlier in the month I felt almost lit up and unstoppable, then I’d snap at my mom or my supervisor over little questions that normally wouldn’t bother me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the charged-up stretch involved an unusually energized or 'up' mood compared with normal, which directly corresponds to elevated/irritable mood.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I did. It’s hard to describe without making it sound like I was just in a good mood, because it wasn’t exactly that. It was more like I felt almost lit up, like everything in me was turned up higher than usual. I remember thinking, “Okay, I’ve got this, I can handle everything,” like I was suddenly unstoppable or something.

And at first that felt kind of good, honestly, especially compared to now. Like I had more confidence than I normally do, and things felt more possible. But it wasn’t just happy or positive. I was also really quick to get irritated. My mom would ask me a normal question, something small, and I’d snap back like she was accusing me of something. Or my supervisor would ask about some little detail at work, and I’d feel this flash of anger, like, “Why are you on me about this?” even though normally I probably would’ve just answered.

So yes, I was more “up,” but also kind of edgy with it. Not calm energy. More like I was running hot.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated/irritable period included decreased need for sleep, which would strongly support a bipolar-spectrum episode over depression, anxiety, stress-related disorder, or primary insomnia.
doctor.question: During that more charged-up stretch, did you need less sleep than usual and still feel okay the next day?

target_item.name: Decreased_Sleep
target_item.manifestation: There were several nights I only slept three or four hours and still got up feeling charged, like coffee wasn’t even necessary.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, during the charged-up stretch, I needed less sleep than usual and still felt okay the next day, which directly matches decreased need for sleep.

patient.answer:
Yeah. That was one of the weirdest parts, honestly, because normally if I don’t sleep enough, I feel it right away. I’m dragging, I need coffee, I’m kind of useless in the morning.

But during that stretch, there were several nights where I only slept maybe three or four hours, and I still got up feeling… charged, I guess. Like I’d wake up and my body was already going, like I didn’t even need coffee. I remember almost being surprised by it, because I’d look at the time and realize how little I’d slept, but I didn’t feel tired in the way I should have.

It wasn’t like I was resting well, exactly. It was more like sleep just didn’t feel as necessary for a bit, which is not normal for me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated period included increased goal-directed activity, which would help distinguish bipolar spectrum hypomania from stress-related or unipolar depression with insomnia.
doctor.question: During that more charged-up stretch, were you doing more activities or taking on more projects than usual?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: For a while I had this burst of energy where I was cleaning, making renovation lists, checking interest rates, and setting up side-job ideas all after work like I couldn’t shut it off.
target_item.reason: The question asks about doing more activities or taking on more projects during the charged-up stretch, which directly matches increased goal-directed activity or energy.

patient.answer:
Yeah, definitely. That was actually one of the things that made me realize something was off, because it wasn’t just that I had more energy in my head — I was doing a lot more.

I’d get home from work, and normally after staring at numbers all day I want to eat something, maybe watch TV, maybe do one chore if I’m being responsible. But during that stretch, I’d come home and suddenly start cleaning like the place had to be fixed immediately. I’d be wiping down cabinets, sorting things, moving stuff around, like I couldn’t just sit down.

And then because of the condo, I started making all these renovation lists — not even realistic ones, necessarily. Like I’d be writing down what I wanted to change, what it might cost, what order to do things in, looking up supplies, comparing ideas. Then I’d switch over to checking interest rates again, even though the mortgage was already done, like I needed to keep monitoring everything.

And on top of that I started setting up ideas for side jobs, like ways I could bring in extra money. I’d be making notes, looking at options, thinking maybe I could do bookkeeping on the side or organize something online. It was all after work, too. It wasn’t like I had free time. I just kept going like I couldn’t shut it off.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the elevated/energized period was long enough to meet hypomanic criteria and distinguish bipolar spectrum illness from depression, anxiety, stress-related symptoms, or insomnia.
doctor.question: About how many days in a row did that more charged-up period last?

target_item.name: Duration

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how long the more charged-up period lasted, which is a duration/time-course question.

patient.answer:
I’m trying to count it exactly, because it wasn’t like one clean block where I can say, “It started Monday and ended Friday.” The really obvious back-and-forth — like being all charged up and then crashing — has been going on for about a month now, basically since the mortgage became real and it wasn’t just an idea anymore.

The charged-up parts would come in stretches within that, but the whole pattern has been about a month. That’s when I started noticing, or maybe when it became harder to ignore, because everything felt more intense around then.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the elevated periods included abnormally increased talkativeness, which would strengthen bipolar spectrum diagnosis over depression, anxiety, stress-related disorder, or primary insomnia.
doctor.question: During those charged-up periods, were you talking more than usual?

target_item.name: Pressured_Speech
target_item.manifestation: My sister told me I was talking so fast about equity, taxes, and paint colors that she couldn’t get a word in, and I could feel myself pushing to keep going.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, during the charged-up periods, I was talking more than usual, which directly matches pressured speech.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I didn’t notice it at first as “talking more,” exactly, because in my head it felt like I was just explaining things that were important. But my sister definitely noticed.

I remember one conversation where I was going on about the condo stuff, and it was like I jumped from equity to taxes to paint colors and then back to what I should do first, and she finally kind of laughed but also looked overwhelmed and said I was talking really fast. Like she couldn’t even get a word in.

And I could feel it, too, once she pointed it out. It was like there was this pressure behind it, like if I didn’t keep going I’d lose the thread or the idea would disappear. I wasn’t trying to cut her off, but I kept pushing forward, almost like the words were coming faster than I could sort them.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods included grandiosity, which would help distinguish bipolar-spectrum hypomania from stress/anxiety or unipolar depression.
doctor.question: During those charged-up periods, did you feel more confident or capable than usual—to the point that your ideas or abilities seemed unusually strong or special?

target_item.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: I honestly started thinking I could pay the condo down fast, pass the CPA exams, and run a little bookkeeping business on the side like failure just wasn’t an option.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether, during charged-up periods, the patient felt unusually confident or capable, with ideas or abilities seeming especially strong or special, which directly matches inflated self-esteem/grandiosity.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes, I think that’s a good way to put it. At the time it didn’t feel like “I’m being unrealistic” or anything. It felt like I could just handle everything if I pushed hard enough.

I honestly started thinking I could pay the condo down really fast, like way faster than a normal person probably would with my income, and that I’d just figure it out somehow. And then I’d be thinking, okay, I can study for the CPA exams too, even though that’s a huge thing and I haven’t exactly had some perfect plan for it before. But during those charged-up times it was like, no, I can do that, I can pass them, I can move up, I can make more money.

And then I also got really convinced I could run a little bookkeeping business on the side, like after work, and somehow it would all fit together. Condo, extra payments, CPA studying, side clients — in my head it wasn’t even “maybe.” It was more like, of course I can do this, failure just isn’t an option.

Looking back, it feels kind of embarrassing because I know those are big things, and not impossible exactly, but the way I was thinking about them was… too certain. Like I suddenly had this belief that I was much more capable than usual and that if I just kept going, I’d make it all happen.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods caused impulsive or risky behavior, which would help distinguish bipolar spectrum illness from stress-related insomnia/anxiety or unipolar depression.
doctor.question: During those charged-up periods, did you do anything unusually risky or impulsive for you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about unusually risky or impulsive behavior during charged-up periods, but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific item for risky or impulsive activities.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that, honestly. I don’t think there was anything like… clearly dangerous, if that’s what you mean. Like I didn’t do something that immediately makes me think, “Oh, that was reckless.”

But I also keep second-guessing myself, because some things felt impulsive in the moment just because I was moving so fast mentally. Like I’d get an idea and feel this urge to act on it right away, instead of sitting with it or thinking it through the way I normally would. So I guess it depends on what counts as risky.

I don’t have one big example where I can say, “Yes, that was definitely risky.” It was more that I felt less cautious than usual, but I’m not sure I actually did anything that crossed a line.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods lasted at least 4 consecutive days, which is key to distinguishing hypomania/bipolar II from depression, anxiety, stress-related symptoms, or insomnia.
doctor.question: Did any one of those charged-up periods last for 4 days in a row or longer?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: The really obvious cycling between that charged-up stretch and this crash has been going on for about a month, since the mortgage became real.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the charged-up periods, specifically whether they lasted 4 days or longer.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. It’s a little hard for me to pin down cleanly, because it hasn’t felt like one neat episode with a start and stop, if that makes sense. But the really obvious back-and-forth — like being in that charged-up stretch and then kind of crashing afterward — has been going on for about a month now.

It really started once the mortgage became real. Like, once it wasn’t just an abstract condo thing anymore, my brain sort of latched onto it, and since then I’ve noticed the cycling a lot more. So I can’t give you an exact day-by-day answer off the top of my head, but yes, there were definitely stretches in there that felt like they lasted several days, not just one afternoon or one night.

inference.note: Evidence now supports a hypomanic episode lasting at least 4 days with decreased need for sleep, increased activity, pressured/rapid speech, irritability, and inflated confidence, making bipolar II disorder the leading candidate; updated F31.8 to the more specific F31.81.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods caused observable impairment or hospitalization, which best distinguishes hypomania (bipolar II) from stress-related mood changes or unipolar depression with insomnia.
doctor.question: During one of those charged-up periods, did it cause problems at work or in your relationships?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still getting to work, but I’ve made enough reconciliation mistakes that my supervisor pulled me aside, and I’ve been avoiding salsa class and friends because I don’t feel like myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the charged-up periods caused problems at work or in relationships, which is directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah… it has, I think. Not in a dramatic way where I stopped functioning completely, because I’m still showing up to work and doing my job, mostly. But it’s definitely started to show.

At work, I’ve made reconciliation mistakes that I really shouldn’t be making. Like, that’s literally part of what I do, so it’s not the kind of thing I can just brush off as, “Oh, everyone makes mistakes.” I mean, everyone does, obviously, but these were enough that my supervisor pulled me aside and asked what was going on. She wasn’t cruel about it, but it was embarrassing. I felt like I had to act like I was fine, but inside I was kind of panicking because I knew I wasn’t being as careful as I normally am.

And socially… yeah, I’ve been avoiding people more. I usually go to salsa class, and I’ve skipped it, and I’ve been dodging friends or not really answering messages the way I normally would. It’s not that they did anything wrong. I just don’t feel like myself, and I don’t want to have to explain that, or be around people and feel like they can tell something is off with me. So I guess it has caused problems, even if I’ve been trying to keep everything looking normal from the outside.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the elevated periods included increased goal-directed activity severe enough to support hypomania over unipolar depression, anxiety, stress reaction, or primary insomnia.
doctor.question: During those charged-up periods, did other people notice that you were unusually active or driven compared with your normal self?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: For a while I had this burst of energy where I was cleaning, making renovation lists, checking interest rates, and setting up side-job ideas all after work like I couldn’t shut it off.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking whether, during charged-up periods, she was unusually active or driven compared with her normal self, which matches increased goal-directed activity or energy.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I don’t know if anyone said it in those exact words, like, “You’re unusually driven,” but I think it was noticeable because I was doing way more than I normally would after work.

Like for a while I’d come home and instead of just making dinner or watching something and going to bed, I’d suddenly have this burst of energy and I’d start cleaning, then making these detailed renovation lists for the condo, then checking interest rates again, then thinking through side-job ideas and setting things up like I had to do it right then. It wasn’t just one productive evening. It was more like I couldn’t shut it off once I got going.

And I think people could tell because I’d talk about all these plans and jump from one thing to another, and it probably sounded like a lot. I remember feeling almost irritated if someone slowed me down or acted like maybe I should just relax, because to me it felt urgent and important. So… yeah, compared with my normal self, I was definitely more active and kind of driven.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods included increased goal-directed activity severe enough to meet hypomanic criteria and clarify bipolar II versus unipolar depression/anxiety-related insomnia by testing for uncharacteristic spending behavior.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. I mean… I don’t think there was anything huge, like I didn’t go buy a car or max out a credit card or anything like that. But I also feel like my sense of what was “reasonable” got kind of fuzzy during those periods, if that makes sense.

I remember looking at things for the condo and feeling like, “Well, we’re going to need this anyway,” or “This is an investment,” and I’d spend a lot of time comparing prices and putting things in carts. I don’t know that I actually bought a ton of it, though. That’s the part I’d have to check, because some of it was more browsing and planning than actually spending.

So… unusual? Maybe a little, but I don’t have a clear example where I’m like, yes, that was completely out of character and caused a big problem. I’d say I haven’t noticed anything major with spending, at least not the way the other stuff has stood out.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated periods reached full mania rather than hypomania by assessing need for hospitalization, which would distinguish bipolar I from bipolar II and help narrow the diagnosis.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about hospitalization for mood or behavior during charged-up periods, and the provided symptom profile does not include any item about hospitalization or inpatient treatment.

patient.answer:
No… I’ve never been hospitalized for it. I mean, there have been times where I felt like I wasn’t handling things well, and I’ve gotten scared by how unlike myself I felt, but it never got to the point where I was taken to a hospital or admitted or anything like that.

I’ve always still been kind of… keeping it together on the outside, I guess. Maybe not well, but enough that it didn’t become an emergency in that way. So no, no hospitalizations for my mood or behavior.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms represent a major depressive episode, which would best distinguish bipolar II disorder from adjustment disorder or primary insomnia/anxiety.
doctor.question: During this low period, has your appetite changed a lot?

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: My appetite has been off enough that I keep skipping dinner or just eating crackers over my budget notebook, and my work pants feel looser than they did a few weeks ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether appetite has changed during the low period.

patient.answer:
Yeah… it has, actually. I wouldn’t say I’m, like, carefully tracking my meals or my weight, but I’ve noticed I’m just not eating normally.

Dinner is the main thing. I’ll get home and I’ll mean to make something, or I’ll think, “Okay, I should eat,” but then I just don’t really have the appetite for it. Or it feels like too much effort, and I end up just eating crackers or something small while I’m sitting there with my budget notebook open. Like, not even a real meal, just picking at something because I know I should have food in my stomach.

And I can tell it’s not just in my head because my work pants feel looser than they did a few weeks ago. Not dramatically, maybe, but enough that I noticed it when I was getting dressed. So yeah… my appetite has been off, and I think I’ve probably lost some weight, even if I haven’t really weighed myself.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the depressive syndrome has lasted long enough to meet criteria for a major depressive episode, which best separates bipolar II disorder from adjustment disorder, anxiety, and primary insomnia at this point.
doctor.question: For at least 2 weeks in a row, have you felt depressed or lost interest in things most of the day, nearly every day?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Lately I wake up with this heavy, empty feeling, like even sitting in my own condo that I worked so hard for just makes me want to cry.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, for at least two weeks, the patient has had depressed mood or loss of interest most of the day nearly every day. Between the two topics, the question first and most directly asks about depressed mood, which is covered by S024.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes. I think so. It’s been more than two weeks, I’d say, where most days I wake up and there’s just this heavy, empty feeling already there, before anything has even happened.

It’s hard to explain because it’s not always like I’m actively crying all day, but it’s like everything feels flattened and sad underneath. Even being in my condo, which I worked so hard for and used to feel proud of, I’ll just sit there and look around and feel this awful emptiness, like it should make me happy and instead it makes me want to cry.

And it’s not just a bad evening here and there. It’s been pretty constant lately, most of the day. I keep thinking maybe if I get through work or get home or organize something I’ll feel different, but the feeling is still there. So… yeah, I’d say depressed is the word for it.
